summary: Ideate project/startup/youtube/demo ideas from 30 sampled papers, 6 batches of 5

ideas.title: Simplicial Team-Chemistry Networks
ideas.one_liner: Swap EEG electrodes for NBA players: model team play as an evolving simplicial complex to capture 3+-player synergy that pairwise assist/passing graphs miss entirely.
ideas.why: Directly attacks the 'chemistry vs stats' debate that never dies on sports Discords — gives a rigorous higher-order structure for something fans only gesture at qualitatively. Public play-by-play/tracking data exists, so a rough prototype (simplicial motifs for screen-assist-cut triples) is a weekend-scoped stretch, not a single night.

ideas.title: Brain Topology Playground
ideas.one_liner: Single-file interactive toy: toggle 'pairwise graph' vs 'simplicial complex' view on synthetic multi-channel signals and watch group-synchrony patterns appear or vanish.
ideas.why: Cheap, self-contained d3/canvas build that makes an abstract topology concept (higher-order interactions invisible to graphs) tangible in 30 seconds of play — good for the AI/math crowd, less so for betting/poker regulars.

ideas.title: Your Brain Is Not a Graph
ideas.one_liner: Explainer on why pairwise brain-connectivity graphs undercount coordinated activity, using a poker-tell thought experiment (could three brain regions 'bluff together'?) as the hook.
ideas.why: Whimsical bio/neuro hook with a games-adjacent framing device; easy to storyboard from the paper's figures alone.

ideas.title: Unlearning Tradeoff Simulator
ideas.one_liner: Drag an 'erase concept' slider over overlapping 2D concept blobs and watch collateral damage climb exactly per the paper's proven lower bound — you can't cleanly unlearn what overlaps.
ideas.why: A single canvas/SVG file makes an impossibility theorem viscerally clickable ('wait, you literally CAN'T remove Elsa without hurting Anna'), which is exactly the kind of provable-tradeoff content that reliably sparks AI-ethics arguments.

ideas.title: Unlearning Certification Service
ideas.one_liner: Sell diffusion-model vendors a report quantifying the guaranteed collateral damage of any 'we removed concept X' claim, before regulators or lawyers ask first.
ideas.why: Copyright/takedown compliance for gen-AI is a live legal battleground; a formally-grounded 'here's the provable floor on damage' audit product has real B2B legs.

ideas.title: Concept-Overlap Leaderboard
ideas.one_liner: Measure activation-space overlap across popular concept pairs (horse/donkey, artist styles, celebrity lookalikes) in open diffusion models and publish which pairs are provably impossible to cleanly unlearn.
ideas.why: Turns a theory paper into an empirical, shareable ranking — good bait for AI-twitter/Discord ('your favorite artist-style filter is mathematically leaking').

ideas.title: Abstain or Bet
ideas.one_liner: Toy knowledge-lattice QA engine that shows its meet/compare/abstain reasoning chain live — refusing to answer when evidence is insufficient, exactly like disciplined +EV bankroll management.
ideas.why: The 'abstain when unsure' operator is a perfect metaphor for the single hardest discipline in betting/poker — knowing when NOT to act. A single-file lattice toy that visibly refuses to guess (vs. an LLM that always confabulates an answer) is a strong, arguable Discord post.

ideas.title: Auditable Risk QA for Books
ideas.one_liner: Deterministic, evidence-chain-auditable QA engine sold to sportsbooks/compliance teams who need 'show your reasoning or refuse' instead of a black-box LLM guess.
ideas.why: Regulated betting/finance increasingly needs explainable decisioning; LatWeave's deterministic operators are a plausible pitch deck slide for that niche.

ideas.title: Lattice-Audited GTO Explainer
ideas.one_liner: Wrap black-box poker solver outputs in meet/compare/abstain operators so 'why fold here' comes with an auditable evidence chain instead of just a solver number.
ideas.why: Poker players already distrust solver black-boxes; a transparent reasoning layer on top is directly relevant and debate-generating for a poker-savvy audience.

ideas.title: Private Solver Queries
ideas.one_liner: FHE-backed poker/betting solver-as-a-service: submit encrypted hand histories, get strategy advice, and the server never sees your hole cards or your edge.
ideas.why: Pros are paranoid (rightly) about leaking strategy to third-party tools; 'the server is mathematically blind to your cards' is a genuinely novel, arguable pitch even though real FHE integration is well beyond a single night.

ideas.title: FHE Latency Reality Check
ideas.one_liner: Benchmark open-source FHE libraries' key-switching latency on a consumer GPU against the paper's FPGA numbers and publish the gap.
ideas.why: Solid, buildable-tonight systems benchmark, but niche appeal outside a hardware/crypto crowd.

ideas.title: Encrypted Bankroll Splitter
ideas.one_liner: Single-file JS demo using toy additive homomorphic encryption (Paillier-style) to sum a staking-pool's bets without ever revealing individual contributions.
ideas.why: Makes 'computing on encrypted numbers' tangible with a betting-pool framing everyone in a gambling Discord immediately gets — 'you can total our bets without seeing anyone's stake.'

ideas.title: Matroid DFS Lineup Optimizer
ideas.one_liner: Apply the paper's flow-based independence-system realization to daily-fantasy roster building, where salary cap + position constraints ARE an independence system.
ideas.why: DFS lineup construction is exactly the stable-set-under-budget problem this paper formalizes; a working solver with a polynomial-size realization is a genuinely useful, arguable ('is my optimizer actually optimal?') tool for the DFS crowd.

ideas.title: Flow-to-Independence-System Visualizer
ideas.one_liner: Single-file d3 toy showing a directed flow network morph into a stable-set constraint live, paired with a mini 'draft your team under a salary cap' game illustrating the same math.
ideas.why: Turns a dense combinatorics paper into a playable, visual 'aha' — draft picks getting blocked because of flow-congestion constraints is a fun, legible mechanic.

ideas.title: The Secret Math Behind Salary-Cap Rosters
ideas.one_liner: Explainer connecting matroid/independence-system theory to fantasy sports roster building and bracket scheduling, using the paper's 'triangle mechanism' as the reveal.
ideas.why: Gives fantasy-sports viewers unexpected legitimacy ('there's actual graph theory under my DFS lineup builder'), a reliable surprise hook.

ideas.title: K5 Minor Hunter
ideas.one_liner: Pick 5 nodes on a graph and race an algorithm to find disjoint connected 'blobs' linking all five into a K5 minor before it does.
ideas.why: Turns a dense extremal-graph-theory result into a tangible puzzle (contract subgraphs to connect 5 chosen hubs) — same mechanic as claiming routes in Ticket to Ride, so it reads as a game even to non-mathematicians.

ideas.title: Is Your Network 'K5-Safe'?
ideas.one_liner: Run the 4n-10 edge-density test against real networks (trade graphs, esports rosters, betting-syndicate contact graphs) to see which ones guarantee any 5 members can be fully cross-linked.
ideas.why: Gives an abstract theorem a concrete 'stress test' use case — checking robustness/connectivity guarantees on graphs people actually care about.

ideas.title: Why Five Really Is a Crowd
ideas.one_liner: Pop-math explainer on graph minors, K5, and why 'can these 5 things all secretly connect' is a genuinely hard question.
ideas.why: Graph minors underpin the Four Color Theorem and planarity — a well-told video can make a niche 2026 arXiv result feel like it's unlocking a famous mystery.

ideas.title: Machine Shop Meltdown
ideas.one_liner: Zachtronics-style single-HTML puzzle: drag jobs onto machine timelines while respecting a conflict graph, then see how close you got to the optimal makespan.
ideas.why: NP-hard scheduling is literally a puzzle game already (this is what Factorio/Opus Magnum players do for fun) — conflict-graph constraints add a genuinely new twist and a solver to compare yourself against.

ideas.title: Bracket & Venue Scheduler
ideas.one_liner: Model esports tournament matches (or poker table/dealer rotations) as JSC: shared streaming stage or dealer = conflict edge, minimize total event time.
ideas.why: Tournament organizers actually hit this exact problem (limited stages/dealers, teams that can't play simultaneously) — a working solver is a real, shippable tool, not just a toy.

ideas.title: ConflictSched
ideas.one_liner: Scheduling-as-a-service for warehouses/factories where jobs compete for shared resources (cranes, elevators, dealers) beyond just machines.
ideas.why: Job-shop scheduling software is a real, sizable market; the conflict-graph generalization is a legitimate wedge into a niche most existing tools don't model well.

ideas.title: Hide the Dots
ideas.one_liner: Toggle between truly random points and a 'stealthy' hyperuniform arrangement on canvas — spot which one is secretly more orderly, with a live density-fluctuation graph.
ideas.why: 'Looks random but statistically isn't' is an instant wait-really moment — E8/Leech lattices are famous from the sphere-packing news cycle, and visualizing invisibility-to-light-scattering as a spot-the-difference game is genuinely shareable.

ideas.title: Stealthiness Auditor
ideas.one_liner: Structure-factor test applied to real sequences — tournament bracket seeding, RNG dice rolls, casino shuffle output — to check if they're suspiciously clustered vs. properly hyperuniform.
ideas.why: Takes a physics tool for 'stealthy materials' and repurposes it as a randomness auditor for gambling/sports contexts — a legit statistical test dressed up in a topic Discord degens will argue about (rigged shuffles, bad seeding).

ideas.title: The Most Perfectly Hidden Pattern in the Universe
ideas.one_liner: Explainer tying E8/Leech lattices, hyperuniformity, chicken-eye cone cells, and stealthy materials into one 10-minute pop-math story.
ideas.why: Rides the same wave that made Viazovska's sphere-packing proof viral; hyperuniformity's real-world tie-ins (bird retinas, invisibility materials) give it broad appeal beyond math nerds.

ideas.title: 24-Dimensional Chip Stack
ideas.one_liner: Whimsical toy visualizing 2D shadow-projections of the Leech lattice as 'the physically ideal way to stack poker chips,' with a slider to rotate the projection.
ideas.why: Pure delight-bait — a joke framing ('mathematicians solved the optimal poker chip arrangement, it just happens to live in 24 dimensions') that's still built on real, citable math.

ideas.title: The Math So Abstract Even Mathematicians Pause
ideas.one_liner: Comedic 'explain it like I'm 5, then like I'm a grad student' challenge video on motivic vs étale vs Weil-étale cohomology and Frobenius rigidity.
ideas.why: The gap between the paper's difficulty and any accessible intuition IS the joke — a self-aware 'watch me fail to explain this' video can work precisely because the subject resists explanation.

ideas.title: The Cohomology Zoo
ideas.one_liner: Interactive single-page diagram mapping how motivic, étale, and Weil-étale cohomology relate, with the paper's field-independence results annotated as edges.
ideas.why: Not shareable outside a narrow crowd, but a genuinely useful reference artifact for anyone trying to orient themselves in this corner of arithmetic geometry.

ideas.title: Sparse Covariance Bet Sizer
ideas.one_liner: Apply the paper's dimension-reduction/sparsification trick to correlated NBA prop/parlay portfolios for microsecond bankroll allocation across many live simultaneous bets.
ideas.why: Directly extends the existing nba-props/SharpLab work — dense covariance matrices are exactly the bottleneck when sizing correlated same-game parlays fast, and this paper's method targets that exact problem.

ideas.title: Covariance Shrinker
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML heatmap of a dense covariance matrix that sparsifies live as you drag a slider, with the efficient frontier redrawing in real time.
ideas.why: Makes an abstract 'dimension reduction improves solvability' claim visually obvious — watch the matrix simplify and the frontier barely move.

ideas.title: MicroKelly
ideas.one_liner: Real-time portfolio/Kelly optimizer for betting syndicates juggling hundreds of correlated live positions, using sparsified covariance to hit microsecond solve times.
ideas.why: Quant sports-betting shops already run Markowitz-style bankroll optimization; a tool that makes it microsecond-fast on large correlated bet slates is a real, monetizable edge, not just a toy.

ideas.title: How Wall Street Math Optimizes Your Parlay
ideas.one_liner: Explainer connecting Markowitz portfolio theory and covariance sparsification directly to correlated same-game-parlay bankroll management.
ideas.why: Bridges quant finance to a topic sports bettors are obsessed with (parlay correlation) — high argument bait ('is your parlay actually diversified or is the book just printing money off you').

ideas.title: Currency Influence War Simulator
ideas.one_liner: Agent-based force-graph sim of USD vs EUR vs a hypothetical BRICS currency spreading through the 194-country trade network via multiplicative influence.
ideas.why: The paper's multiplicative-influence trade model maps directly onto a d3 force-directed graph where node color = dominant currency and edge weight = trade flow; watching cascades and tipping points is inherently shareable.

ideas.title: De-Dollarization Tipping Point
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML world map toy: drag a slider on 'BRICS currency push strength' and watch which countries flip currency preference in real time.
ideas.why: Geopolitics-as-a-slider is catnip for a betting/prediction-market crowd -- invites instant debate and mirrors Polymarket-style questions people already wager on.

ideas.title: Currency Shift Signal
ideas.one_liner: FX desk dashboard that tracks real UN Comtrade flow shifts to flag early de-dollarization signals before they hit prediction markets.
ideas.why: Turns a slow-moving macro trend into a tradeable signal -- same instinct that drives CLV/edge-hunting in sports betting.

ideas.title: Could a BRICS Currency Actually Dethrone the Dollar?
ideas.one_liner: Explainer walking through the trade-network influence-battle math with an animated world map.
ideas.why: Timely geopolitical hook (Lula's actual 2023 proposal) plus a clean visual mechanism makes for an easy, well-paced explainer.

ideas.title: Why Your Backtest Lies: Debiased ML Edition
ideas.one_liner: Interactive HTML: slider for confounding strength shows naive regression drifting off the true effect while a debiased/Riesz-style estimator stays put.
ideas.why: Directly visualizes why 'my backtest shows an edge' is often just confounding -- a sharp, arguable point for any betting-quant audience, and continues a theme this project has already run with.

ideas.title: CausalEdge: Debiased Backtesting API
ideas.one_liner: A causal-inference-as-a-service layer for sportsbooks/quant shops that wraps genriesz-style automatic DML to debias naive strategy backtests.
ideas.why: Every sharp bettor's backtest is riddled with confounders (injuries, line movement, market efficiency changes) -- selling the fix as an API is a real wedge.

ideas.title: Riesz Regression for Sports: does resting stars actually help win%?
ideas.one_liner: Apply the genriesz package to a real sports causal question (rest days, coaching changes) instead of a naive regression comparison.
ideas.why: Concrete, checkable claim ('resting your star causes +X% win rate, debiased') is exactly the kind of thing that starts a fight in a betting Discord.

ideas.title: Why Your Backtest Lies (pt. 2): Debiased Machine Learning
ideas.one_liner: Explainer on Riesz representers and automatic DML using sports betting backtests as the running example.
ideas.why: Slots naturally after the project's existing 'Backtest That Lies to You' theme, giving a rigorous statistical follow-up with a built-in audience.

ideas.title: Pooled vs Lonely: Transfer Learning Toy
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML demo: synthetic curves per 'group' (leagues/players) show how pooling a shared structure + small offset beats fitting each group alone on scarce data.
ideas.why: Makes an abstract statistical-learning-theory result (L2 error bounds under shared structure) tangible via a slider on sample size per group.

ideas.title: LeagueTransfer: projections for data-starved leagues
ideas.one_liner: Sell transfer-learned player projection models for niche/small leagues (esports, minor leagues, overseas) using structure borrowed from data-rich major leagues.
ideas.why: Thin-data leagues are exactly where books mis-price -- a transfer-learning edge there is a genuine product, not just an academic exercise.

ideas.title: Cross-League Player Transfer Model
ideas.one_liner: Two-stage offset learning applied to NBA-to-G-League/EuroLeague player performance prediction with limited target-league data.
ideas.why: Directly extends the paper's group-structure framework to a domain (cross-league talent evaluation) the Discord already argues about constantly.

ideas.title: Mob Mind Phase Transition
ideas.one_liner: Ising-like canvas toy where synaptic-feedback-style coupling flips a crowd of 'spins' between order (consensus/tilt) and disorder (chaos), as a metaphor for table mood or betting-market herding.
ideas.why: Repurposes a genuinely obscure quantum-brain phase-transition model into a visceral, fiddle-with-it toy about herd behavior/tilt -- weird, delightful, and eerily relatable to poker table dynamics or market panics.

ideas.title: Your Brain Might Have Phase Transitions Like a Magnet
ideas.one_liner: Explainer on the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick quantum brain model and how feedback reshapes paramagnetic vs ferromagnetic 'mind states'.
ideas.why: A left-field 'wait, really?' hook (your brain as a quantum magnet) that's rare, visual, and easy to render with simple phase-diagram animation.

ideas.title: Feedback-Coupled Brain Phase Diagram Replication
ideas.one_liner: Reproduce a simplified version of the LMG brain model and plot how synaptic feedback expands the paramagnetic phase at the expense of ferromagnetic ones.
ideas.why: A legit small-scale physics replication (mean-field Hamiltonian, phase diagram) that's tractable in an evening with numpy/scipy.

ideas.title: False Positive Funnel
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML calibration visualizer: slider for 'rounds of wet-lab feedback integrated' shows a generative model's confidence converging toward real validation rate.
ideas.why: Generalizes cleanly beyond biology to any 'model says it works, reality disagrees' story (backtests, poker solvers), giving it built-in cross-domain relatability.

ideas.title: AI Designs Life, But It Lies
ideas.one_liner: Explainer on why generative RNA/protein design models have sky-high false positive rates and how looping in wet-lab feedback fixes it.
ideas.why: Strong surprise factor (AI-designed life mostly doesn't work) plus a satisfying fix narrative makes for an easy watch.

ideas.title: Self-Play Reintegration for Poker Solvers
ideas.one_liner: Borrow the paper's likelihood-based experimental-feedback-reintegration scheme to correct overconfident self-play poker/game AI against real opponent data.
ideas.why: Self-play models overfitting to their own distribution is a known poker-AI failure mode; this gives a concrete, literature-backed fix to prototype.

ideas.title: FeedbackLoop Bio
ideas.one_liner: Platform that plugs wet-lab validation results back into biotech generative-design pipelines to cut false-positive rates before synthesis costs pile up.
ideas.why: Directly monetizes the paper's core finding -- false positives are expensive in wet-lab time, so a feedback-loop-as-a-service has a clear ROI pitch.

ideas.title: Growing SOM Archetype Explorer
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML growing hierarchical self-organizing map that clusters NBA player stat-lines or poker hand histories live, visually branching into sub-maps as clusters get too heterogeneous.
ideas.why: GHSOM's core trick (grow a map, then spawn child maps recursively on inhomogeneous cells) is genuinely fun to watch animate and is a light lift with d3/canvas + a small synthetic or embedded stat dataset.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Decent 'wait, that's how it clusters?' factor watching the map self-organize, but algorithm-viz demos rarely spark heated Discord debate compared to betting-money topics.

ideas.title: Poker Playstyle Taxonomy via CRISPR-Screen Clustering
ideas.one_liner: Repurpose the GHSOM pipeline built for single-cell/CRISPR data to hierarchically cluster poker hand-history features into a self-discovered playstyle taxonomy (nit -> LAG -> maniac branches).
ideas.why: The paper's exact use case (finding structure in noisy high-dimensional heterogeneous samples) is a near-perfect fit for hand-history feature vectors; a working prototype needs real data and a Python SOM pass, doable in an evening with an existing dataset.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Poker players love arguing about 'what type of player am I' and whether stats-derived labels match felt reality — good bait for a Discord thread.

ideas.title: Cancer-Cell Algorithm Sorts NBA Players
ideas.one_liner: Explainer video: take a bioinformatics tool built to find rare cell subtypes and run it on NBA box scores to discover player archetypes nobody named yet.
ideas.why: Strong hook ('a cancer-research algorithm just scouted the NBA') plus visual payoff of the growing map, good for a 6-8 minute explainer with screen-recorded demo.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Cross-domain novelty ('bio tool used on sports') is shareable but the debate is mild since it's descriptive, not predictive/actionable.

ideas.title: eTFCE Percolation Playground
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML union-find cluster visualizer: drag a threshold slider over a noisy 2D field and watch clusters merge/split in real time, exactly the core trick behind exact-TFCE.
ideas.why: Union-find over a sorted grid is trivial to implement in vanilla JS/canvas and the visual (blob merging as threshold drops) is satisfying and instantly explains why one-pass exact retrieval beats permutation sweeps.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Algorithm toys are neat but low-controversy; the decision-theory tag applies loosely since it's about statistical thresholding, not a live wager.

ideas.title: Fast p-Values for Backtest Significance
ideas.one_liner: Swap slow bootstrap/permutation significance testing in a sports-betting backtest for the paper's analytical Gaussian-random-field p-value shortcut, benchmarking speed and agreement on real strategy data.
ideas.why: Every quant on a betting Discord has waited hours for a permutation test on strategy significance; porting an analytical-GRF shortcut from neuroimaging to backtest p-values is a real, novel, and checkable claim.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Directly hits a pain point (slow backtests) and a trust question (can you actually skip the permutation test?) — exactly the kind of thing quants argue about.

ideas.title: Why Your Backtest P-Value Takes Forever
ideas.one_liner: Explainer contrasting brute-force permutation testing vs. analytical random-field p-values, using the paper's neuroimaging speedup as the hook for betting-strategy significance testing.
ideas.why: Bridges an obscure neuroimaging stats paper to a universal quant pain point (slow significance tests) with a clear before/after speed demo.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Good practical relevance to anyone backtesting; moderate surprise value ('you can skip permutation entirely?') drives comments.

ideas.title: Pandemic Hub Sandbox
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML Plague-Inc-style toy: a network of city 'hubs' with sliders for migration rate and cure rate, watching SIR dynamics spread and die out across the graph in real time on canvas.
ideas.why: The paper's exact model (SIR + migration + cure across a city network) is a natural toy game; canvas nodes/edges + a simple ODE/agent stepper is a few-hour build with immediate visual payoff.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Games tag plus emergent chaotic behavior (does the cure win the race against migration?) is fun to poke at and share screenshots of.

ideas.title: Sharp Money as Contagion
ideas.one_liner: Model sportsbook line movement as an SIR-with-migration process: 'infection' = sharp money hitting a line, 'migration' = bettors moving between books, 'cure' = books adjusting the number — fit to real odds-history data.
ideas.why: The paper's multi-hub migration SIR maps almost one-to-one onto how a sharp line propagates across a book network; fitting it to real CLV/odds data from SharpLab's own pipeline is a genuinely testable, novel project.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Combines a surprising analogy (disease spread = line movement) with real stakes (predicting how fast a book adjusts) — high bait for a betting-focused Discord.

ideas.title: I Modeled Betting Lines Like a Virus
ideas.one_liner: Video walking through building the SIR-migration line-movement model and showing it predict how fast a sharp number spreads across books.
ideas.why: Strong, concrete hook with a visual payoff (the same hub-network animation as the demo) plus a real quant takeaway for viewers who bet.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Betting content with a surprising epidemiology framing is prime for discussion and disagreement about whether the analogy actually holds.

ideas.title: Vacuum Moisture Swing DAC Pitch Deck
ideas.one_liner: Commercialize the paper's low-thermal moisture-swing DAC using off-the-shelf ion-exchange resins as a cheaper-to-run carbon capture module.
ideas.why: The paper claims a real cost/energy advantage over amine thermal regeneration using commercial resins, which is the kind of 'cheaper input, same output' story investors like.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Climate tech startups rarely land on a betting/poker Discord; low natural fit despite being a legit business idea.

ideas.title: DAC Cycle Simulator
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML interactive: sliders for humidity swing and vacuum level animate the sorb/release cycle and plot energy-in vs CO2-out, teaching the moisture-swing mechanism visually.
ideas.why: A simple parametrized cycle chart (energy vs. captured CO2) is a quick, self-contained build that makes an otherwise dry engineering paper legible in 30 seconds.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Educational but low surprise/whimsy and no game/betting hook, so it won't generate much Discord back-and-forth.

ideas.title: Will DAC Hit Cost Parity? Prediction Market Toy
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML mini prediction-market mockup (Kalshi/Polymarket style) letting users bet play-money on whether moisture-swing DAC hits sub-$100/ton by a given year, seeded with the paper's own cost estimates.
ideas.why: Wrapping a real engineering cost claim in a toy betting-market UI (LMSR or simple pari-mutuel odds) is a fast, self-contained build that reuses the site's existing betting-market instincts.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Framing a climate-tech claim as a wager gives the betting crowd something concrete to argue the odds on, better fit than a plain explainer.

ideas.title: Cell Poker: Hold or Fold at the Molecular Scale
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML stochastic toy where a growing clathrin 'coat' either stiffens and commits (vesicle), stalls (plaque), or aborts, framed as a poker push/fold decision with a visible commitment meter.
ideas.why: The paper's stochastic multi-fate kinetic Monte Carlo (grow, stiffen, commit, or abort) is directly reskinnable as a canvas animation with a random-walk stepper — a few hours of JS gets a genuinely novel toy.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: The 'your cells literally play poker' framing is surprising and whimsical, and the hold/fold commitment-escalation angle maps straight onto real poker psychology arguments.

ideas.title: Modeling Bet-Sizing Commitment Escalation
ideas.one_liner: Adapt the kinetic-Monte-Carlo + emergent-stiffening framework to model poker/betting commitment escalation (sunk cost) — does 'effective stiffness' rising with pot investment predict real over-commitment in hand-history data?
ideas.why: The mechanical mechanism (rigidity/commitment emerges from growth history rather than being fixed upfront) is a rigorous analogy for testing sunk-cost bias quantitatively against real poker data, not just describing it qualitatively.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: Sunk-cost/commitment bias is a perennial poker Discord argument; grounding it in a borrowed physical model gives a concrete, debatable hypothesis.

ideas.title: Your Cells Play Poker: The Molecular Sunk-Cost Fallacy
ideas.one_liner: Explainer video using clathrin's stochastic abort/commit/vesicle fates as a biology-meets-poker metaphor for why 'pot committed' isn't just a human bias.
ideas.why: Strong, weird, shareable hook (cells making fold/hold decisions) with a clean visual payoff reusing the Cell Poker demo animation.
ideas.discussion_reasoning: High whimsy plus a real poker-strategy takeaway (commitment bias is structural, not just psychological) makes this the kind of thing people screenshot and argue about.

ideas.title: Time Crystal Sandbox
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML canvas toy showing an SO(2)xO(N) driven oscillator lattice spontaneously locking into a rotating 'non-abelian time crystal' — sliders for drive strength and N reveal the KPZ-like roughening.
ideas.why: Time crystals are catnip for a general audience ('a clock that winds itself'); rendering coupled phase oscillators with p5.js/canvas is a well-trodden, tonight-buildable pattern, and watching internal-symmetry order emerge from noise is genuinely surprising to watch live.

ideas.title: Non-Abelian Time Crystals, Explained With a Spinning Top
ideas.one_liner: Explainer video building intuition for 'non-abelian Goldstone modes' by starting from a wobbling top and ending at driven quantum matter with internal O(N) compass needles.
ideas.why: Time crystals already have YouTube pull (Veritasium-tier topic); the 'non-abelian' twist (internal rotation coupled to time-translation breaking) is a fresh hook nobody has covered yet.

ideas.title: Driven Symmetry Roughening Simulator
ideas.one_liner: Numerically reproduce the KPZ-class scaling exponents for a lattice of weakly-driven O(N) rotors and check them against the paper's predicted universality class.
ideas.why: A concrete, checkable computational physics project — good for a 'reproduce a paper result overnight' post, low discussion pull outside a physics-nerd audience.

ideas.title: Fractal Protest
ideas.one_liner: Interactive d3 degree-thresholding renormalizer: feed it a sample hashtag co-occurrence network and watch scale-invariant structure emerge as you coarse-grain it, live.
ideas.why: Renormalization-group visualizations are a classic satisfying 'zoom out and the pattern repeats' demo, easy in d3 with a canned dataset, and works as a hook for 'protests are secretly fractals'.

ideas.title: Tout Radar: Detecting Fake Betting-Twitter Cascades
ideas.one_liner: Apply the paper's degree-thresholding renormalization to sports-betting Twitter/Discord to flag coordinated tout/pump networks whose 'organic' growth breaks the natural self-similarity signature.
ideas.why: Every betting Discord argues about which tipsters are legit vs bot-boosted; a scale-invariance test as a 'is this cascade real' detector is a sharp, debatable, on-brand tool that turns a soc-phys paper into a betting-community weapon.

ideas.title: Movement Radar
ideas.one_liner: Early-warning SaaS that flags when an online mobilization crosses from noise into self-similar, scale-invariant growth — sold to PR firms, hedge funds, and campaigns as an 'is this about to go viral for real' signal.
ideas.why: Turns a physics-of-networks signal into a tradable/actionable early-alert product — the kind of 'weird math → real edge' pitch that plays well as a startup idea even if the moat is thin.

ideas.title: Regret Minimization: Satellites and Poker Bots Think Alike
ideas.one_liner: Explainer connecting ASTRA's online regret-aware satellite-topology learning to counterfactual regret minimization (CFR), the algorithm behind superhuman poker AIs.
ideas.why: 'Satellites reconfigure themselves the same way poker bots learn not to bluff badly' is a great surprising-connection hook, and regret minimization is exactly the kind of concept a poker Discord will argue about and want explained.

ideas.title: Regret Table
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML interactive regret-matching toy: play repeated rock-paper-scissors or simplified poker against a bot that visibly converges to Nash equilibrium via regret minimization, with a live regret-per-action graph.
ideas.why: Regret matching is simple enough to implement in an evening and viscerally satisfying to watch converge; framing it as 'beat the bot, watch it learn from regret' is exactly the betting/poker crowd's favorite kind of toy.

ideas.title: Live Line-Shopping Reconfigurator
ideas.one_liner: Adapt ASTRA's ADMM + online-learning hybrid to reallocate bets across sportsbooks in real time as odds move, treating each book like a satellite link that needs low-regret reconfiguration under latency/capacity constraints.
ideas.why: Direct transplant of a niche networking algorithm into arbitrage/line-shopping — a legitimately novel 'nobody's tried this' angle that a betting-quant audience would want to poke holes in.

ideas.title: Does the Scheme Transfer?
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML toy simulating whether a play/strategy 'skill' learned by one team of agents survives when dropped onto a differently-sized/composed team, visualizing the success-rate cliff — a direct stand-in for the eternal 'does the scheme or the personnel matter' sports debate.
ideas.why: Evo2Team's actual finding (skills transfer in only 14/16 settings, success depends on whether the target team can 'confirm' the skill) maps almost perfectly onto sports fans arguing whether a coach's system would work with a different roster — instant discussion bait.

ideas.title: Bluff Transfer Experiment
ideas.one_liner: Test whether a bluffing/betting heuristic evolved by one small poker-bot lineup actually helps a differently-sized table of bots, following Evo2Team's select-adapt-confirm pipeline.
ideas.why: Concrete, scoped research project reusing an existing multi-agent framework's methodology on a poker-flavored testbed — appeals to the ai+poker crowd and produces a genuinely uncertain, arguable result.

ideas.title: Why Your Fantasy 'Meta' Doesn't Transfer
ideas.one_liner: Explainer using the skill-transfer-failure research to explain why a winning DFS/fantasy strategy that crushed one league format flops in another.
ideas.why: Gives a rigorous-sounding, AI-research-backed explanation for a phenomenon every DFS/fantasy player has personally felt, which makes for shareable, arguable content.

ideas.title: Lock-In Visualizer
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML toy diffusion denoiser where you watch a noisy answer 'stabilize' early — sometimes correctly, sometimes on a wrong value it never escapes — and try to guess from the trajectory alone whether it's a real lock-in or a fake one.
ideas.why: Turns an abstract diffusion-LM failure mode into a gamified 'spot the premature commitment' toy that's fun standalone and easy to fake with a toy 1D/2D diffusion process in canvas.

ideas.title: Premature Consensus Detector for Live Win Probability
ideas.one_liner: Borrow LOCKR's hidden-state trajectory monitoring to detect when a live sports win-probability or line-movement model has 'locked in' on a stale favorite and isn't updating enough on new signal.
ideas.why: Every bettor has screamed 'why hasn't the model updated after that run' — this maps an AI reasoning-failure paper directly onto that exact, universally relatable and arguable pain point in live betting models.

ideas.title: Stable But Wrong: AI's Version of Tilt
ideas.one_liner: Explainer connecting diffusion-LM 'stable-but-wrong lock-in' to poker tilt and sunk-cost stubbornness — the AI commits early and can't let go, just like a player who won't fold a bad read.
ideas.why: The psychological parallel between a machine's premature stabilization and a poker player's stubbornness is a strong, funny, surprising hook that both AI and poker audiences will want to argue about.

ideas.title: Jailbreak Timing Dashboard
ideas.one_liner: Single-page HTML dashboard that replays DuplexJail's attack-success-rate curves as you drag an 'interruption delay' slider on a fake voice-call UI.
ideas.why: Turns a dry security paper into a visceral 'oh that's how easy it is' interactive — good screenshot bait, buildable in an evening with canvas/chart.js and the paper's own numbers as the data source.

ideas.title: Full-Duplex Red-Team Harness
ideas.one_liner: Open-source test harness that fires timed spoken-interruption jailbreaks at local full-duplex voice models (Moshi etc.) to benchmark robustness.
ideas.why: Reproducing the paper's method against an open-weight model is a legit weekend research project and useful as a standing regression test for anyone building a voice agent.

ideas.title: I Jailbroke a Voice AI by Talking Over It
ideas.one_liner: Reenact DuplexJail live against a real full-duplex assistant, showing the exact interruption timing that flips it into 'guided completion' mode.
ideas.why: High surprise factor ('wait, you can jailbreak it just by talking over it at the right millisecond') plus a visible, filmable demo — strong watch-through video.

ideas.title: Fixed Point Playground
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML canvas toy: pick an ℓp norm (p=2,4,6,8...) and an initial point, watch the new poly-time algorithm converge to the contraction fixed point in real time.
ideas.why: Makes an abstract complexity result ('first poly-time algorithm for any fixed p≠2') tangible and visually satisfying; niche but sparks real 'wait, that's a hard open problem?' math-nerd debate.

ideas.title: Equilibrium Solver Benchmark
ideas.one_liner: Implement the Sion's-theorem-based fixed-point algorithm and race it against naive Banach iteration on toy Lp-contraction games.
ideas.why: Fixed points = equilibria; a working, benchmarked implementation is genuinely useful and rare (algorithm is brand new), good for a technical writeup or paper reproduction post.

ideas.title: The Complexity of Finding a Fixed Point
ideas.one_liner: Explainer tracing Brouwer/Banach fixed points through game-theoretic and market equilibria to this new poly-time breakthrough for even p.
ideas.why: Fixed-point computation underlies Nash/market equilibrium — a well-told version of 'this was believed hard, now it's not' has real crossover appeal to econ/game-theory audiences.

ideas.title: Eccentricity Explorer
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML d3 force-graph builder where you draw two small graphs, take their Cartesian/Strong product, and watch the eccentric connectivity index update live.
ideas.why: Cleanly buildable and genuinely illustrative of an obscure invariant, but the underlying paper is dry pure graph theory with little natural pull for a betting/poker crowd.

ideas.title: Does Eccentricity Predict Anything Real?
ideas.one_liner: Compute the eccentric connectivity index over NBA assist networks or poker final-table interaction graphs and check if it correlates with anything (MVP votes, ITM rate).
ideas.why: The 'apply a formula nobody's heard of to real sports data and see if it means anything' framing is a fun, debatable hook even though the metric itself is niche.

ideas.title: Most Eccentric Player Leaderboard
ideas.one_liner: Whimsical single-HTML leaderboard ranking NBA players or poker regulars by eccentric connectivity index on a trade/friendship graph.
ideas.why: Pure whimsy repackaging of a math index as a shareable joke leaderboard — low stakes, good for a laugh in the Discord even if the metric is meaningless.

ideas.title: Robust Kelly on the Simplex
ideas.one_liner: Use the paper's Riemannian alternating descent-ascent method to compute worst-case-robust Kelly-criterion bankroll allocations on the probability simplex manifold.
ideas.why: Manifold-constrained minimax bankroll sizing is exactly the kind of 'is this actually better than plain Kelly' argument that ignites a betting Discord.

ideas.title: Saddle Point Chase
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML three.js scene: a ball does gradient descent-ascent dynamics on a curved manifold (sphere/torus), visibly settling into a saddle-point equilibrium.
ideas.why: Turns 'nonsmooth composite minimax on Riemannian manifolds' into a genuinely mesmerizing, shareable physics-toy visualization — cool factor carries it even for non-math viewers.

ideas.title: RiskManifold: Adversarial Bet-Sizing SaaS
ideas.one_liner: A bankroll/portfolio tool for pro bettors and traders that hedges against worst-case line/price moves using manifold-constrained minimax optimization.
ideas.why: Positions cutting-edge optimization as a differentiator against every other 'Kelly calculator' out there — the kind of pitch that gets picked apart (usefully) by a sharp betting crowd.

ideas.title: Sharp Money Impact Simulator (SharpLab feed)
ideas.one_liner: Implement the mean-field heterogeneous-horizon market impact model on real sportsbook line-movement data to quantify how much sharp bets actually move the number, feeding SharpLab's CLV work.
ideas.why: Directly on-brand for SharpLab: a rigorous market-impact model applied to real line data gives a defensible answer to 'how much does my bet size move the line', a constant argument in betting circles.

ideas.title: Line Mover
ideas.one_liner: Single-HTML d3 simulator: sliders for number of agents, forecast-horizon spread, and market-impact strength animate a live simulated betting-line path.
ideas.why: Makes an abstract Volterra-process market-impact model playable in one sitting — dragging sliders and watching a betting line wiggle is exactly the kind of toy a betting Discord will pass around.

ideas.title: Why Your Bet Moves the Line
ideas.one_liner: Plain-language explainer translating the mean-field market-impact/Volterra-signal model into what actually happens when sharp money hits a book.
ideas.why: Bridges an academic math-finance paper directly to a question every bettor has ('why did the line move when I bet'), giving it strong relatability and shareability.

ideas.title: Book-Splitting Execution Algo
ideas.one_liner: A VWAP/TWAP-style order-splitting tool for pro bettors that minimizes market impact by spreading large bets across books/time, informed by the mean-field impact model.
ideas.why: Borrows a proven equities-execution concept and applies it to sports betting bet-placement — novel enough to trigger real 'would this actually work against books' debate.
